title: Federal Jury Convicts Chinese Telecom Giant Huawei in Sweeping US Criminal Trial
snippet: A Brooklyn federal jury found Huawei guilty of 10 criminal counts, including trade secret theft and sanctions violations, capping a long-running legal battle between Washington and the Chinese tech titan.
content:
NEW YORK — Chinese telecommunications powerhouse Huawei was convicted Tuesday by a federal jury in Brooklyn on 10 criminal counts, concluding a high-stakes legal showdown over U.S. sanctions violations and systemic intellectual property theft.

Following a grueling two-month trial featuring testimony from more than 70 witnesses, jurors found the tech giant guilty of bank fraud, wire fraud, violating international sanctions on Iran, and conspiring to steal trade secrets from American firms. The jury acquitted Huawei on two counts, including racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice.

A Geopolitical Reckoning

The verdict marks a decisive chapter in a sprawling federal prosecution that began in 2018 and fueled intense geopolitical friction between Washington and Beijing. The following year, the U.S. Commerce Department placed Huawei on a trade blacklist over national security concerns, severely restricting its access to American technology.

The saga previously triggered an international crisis in December 2018 when Canadian authorities detained Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer and daughter of its founder, on a U.S. arrest warrant. Meng fought extradition for nearly three years before reaching a deferred prosecution agreement with federal prosecutors and returning to China.

Evidence of Corporate Espionage

Throughout the Brooklyn trial, prosecutors built a case showing that Huawei repeatedly lied to major global banks, including HSBC, to move money in and out of Iran in defiance of U.S. trade restrictions. Prosecutors relied in part on news reports from 2012 and 2013 that exposed the company's covert Iranian operations.

Government lawyers also detailed decades of alleged trade secret theft, presenting evidence that Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems, appropriated wireless antenna designs from Quintel, and improperly accessed semiconductor technology. Jurors were even shown video footage of a Huawei employee placing a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into a backpack, alongside testimony describing an engineer photographing proprietary gear at a competitor's trade show booth.

Defense Vows to Appeal

Defense attorney Brian Heberlig maintained that Huawei built its global empire through genuine innovation and research rather than illicit activity. While expressing disappointment with the guilty counts, Heberlig pointed to the racketeering acquittal as evidence of the firm's compliance efforts.

"We fully expect to appeal," Heberlig told reporters following the verdict, suggesting the absence of a racketeering conviction could significantly impact potential financial penalties.

U.S. District Judge Ann Donnelly will preside over Huawei's sentencing, scheduled for September 14, 2027. Despite Western trade limits, industry analysts observe that Huawei remains a dominant force in Asia, pivoting heavily toward domestic markets and artificial intelligence development.
